Elevator Pitch: A cactus that you can't be near for more than 20 s or else all your romantic relationships will end.

item.title: Seeking Greenlight: The Architects Automaton: Re: Seeking Greenlight: The Architects Automaton
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for the feedback.

Spoiler below

+ show block
– hide block

The reason why It's vague is that it is a mystery note that develops over time. I have to decide between balancing what to say here and what not to spoil in what is effectively the general outline of the story. The problem is that anyone who is actually interested in the concept enough to greenlight it would also end up being spoiled to the story in the long run. I explained in my spoiler post for Cyber exactly why it has the effects it has. It is definitely not just a simple "it drives people insane", but the exact specifics of what it is doing and why it is doing it can fill out 400 words all on it's own and is a huge part of unraveling the mystery that I don't just want to spoil for readers.

In which care, should I care about that at all and just spill everything out?

My ultimate point is already written out as it pertains to the SPC's themselves.
But spoilers kill a story, so I'm not really sure what to do here.
And in my honest opinion, as it pertains to the mystery, I have already said too much in an effort to get greenlit for a sandbox that can't be justified in merely 400 words, but rather should be justified by the reading of the draft article itself.

is the real problem for a story… I would suggest thinking of some other effect seeing the patterns does…

Not a problem at all, because its effects are not random in the slightest and it is not merely just "driving someone insane". The idea here is that everything psychological that seems to be random is actually simply the extreme of things that already exist in the subjects, even in tiny quantities. The idea here is to put on a display that everyone, EVERYONE has some tiny piece of their mind that is not quite right, no matter how small. These patterns have hidden within them traps that latch on and exploit these small problems and cause them to grow to extremes, all in an effort to protect its creator's knowledge. Basically, the machine's patterns are not driving you insane or causing devastating mental diseases, they are simply magnifying the issues that are already there. The idea is that everyone, EVERYONE has some mental issue somewhere, no matter how small they may be. If that's not different enough of a tone then I don't really know what to say there. I'll take it back to the drawing board.

why make people crazy? What else could be done to make it unsettling?

I noted that in the spoiler for Cyber, but that is really the question here. WHY is it doing what it is doing? And the answer is written, but hidden from view because that answer literally answers the mystery of the entire object. I'll probably rewrite or update the greenlight with some spoiler sections explaining the actual story at hand, so that people can read and avoid the context should they care to read along once the story is actually unfolding as an SCP, interviews and experiment logs.

item.title: (Seeking Greenlight) Joke SCP - mind-influencing game code: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Joke SCP - mind-influencing game code
item.content:encoded:
Noting a PM request to take another look

You've, definitely sort of tightened this up so it feels more cohesive as a whole; but it also feels very…flat? I don't really have an idea of like, what you're intending to do with the actual narrative or how the like, situation changes over the course of the story, or what the stakes are or anything. It feels a lot more focussed on -1 as a character but without really like, giving me anything that indicates they're interesting as a character, or like, really…doing anything with the narrative?

You mention that the addendum is about 'the downfall of a Foundation monitoring team': what like, actually happens here? Is this meant as the meat of the article or is this just the appetiser before the main meal of the story?

I missed this the first time round (sorry), but how is this a joke SCP? It feels a lot more like it's 'a serious scp born out of a joke' than 'a scp which is a joke'.

item.title: New SCiP: Just A Very Common Spectroscope (awaiting greenlights): Re: New SCiP: Just A Very Common Spectroscope (awaiting greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

As the energy carried by light will magnify with the shortening of wave length, energy coming from nowhere accumulates in the universe and finally caused… deviation of balance of material and energy. Then unexpected results, like the worst - affect the gradual cosmic expansion or bring near the final collapse.

This feels…like a lot of escalation? Like I get why there's ever growing amounts of energy in the system cos the effects of this changing the wavelength and increasing the energy of light; but it feels…like the universe is so large that this effect would be drowned out by the sheer size of the universe long before it became an actual issue; particularly since you can e.g. put it deep underground with minimal light in the style of a Neutrino Detector.

Even ignoring this, how are you showing this escalation within the article? What do you like, intend to do to convey the threat and have folk try to like, prevent it happening and like, actually get a reader invested in this escalation?

The name 'spectroscope' is probably fine; it's very much the kinda thing you're going to have to describe by like, explaining what it does regardless of name so *shrugs*

Not very sure how to merge the final world-threatening narrative into this ordinary object-describing document. Will a research report (regarding the status of the universe) or a test log work well?

This question raises a lot of concern in me. See, the answer very much depends on what the actual world-threatening narrative is and how you want to tell it: perhaps a series of updates over thousands of years would work if it's slow (see e.g. SCP-4792 for an example of this kind of thing), or some journal entries from a researcher attached to it if you want a quick thing, or some mix of the two. But at it's core, it really just depends on how the story like…unfolds?

item.title: A way to die. (SCP/ Tales idea): A way to die. (SCP/ Tales idea)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article (Maybe a tale too? *More in Additional Notes)

Genre (Optional): Action, Thriller

Page Layout (Optional): Standard SCP layout with quite some addendums (incident report + psychological report + phone call + several Interviews + operational execution Protocol + some more)

Elevator Pitch: My article will tell a story about the SCP Foundation and an SCP struggling to find common ground. SCP-XXXX wants to die, but cant. The Foundation wants to contain it, but is not able to do so. A researcher wants to mediate between these two parties, and pays dearly for the attempt. And with the conflict ongoing, more and more people are being drawn into it.

Central Narrative: SCP-XXXX, one protagonist in the story, has an seemingly simple ability. When dead, its consciousness is transferred in to another body. By that method it is profiting from the knowledge and life experience of every man it has ever bin. Yet it wants to die one last time, tired of the endless life it was gifted, and realises that despite being nearly omniscient, the SCP cant figure out how. In despair it turns to the SCP Foundation that made the fatal error to underrate the SCPs power.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Straightaway it is clear, the SCP Foundation fears SCP-XXXX. But the SCP seems to be completely harmless at its first appearances in the documents. A closer look however reveals, that not its ability is hazardous, but the sheer amount of knowledge it owns about not only science, psychology or self defence, but about the SCP Foundation. Threatened, the Foundation by reflex draws its sword, forgetting that what they attempt to fight is immortal.

Additional Notes: *I, unwisely, already have started a draft without waiting for an reply by qualified reviewers. But when I paused tipping, I noticed that the word counter was already indicating 3000 words (I am not even finished jet), of which only 600 are taken up by the actual SCP document. So I am not only looking for an GREENLIGHT here, but also seek for an experts opinion. Is it just a very long SCP, or would it be better to make it a SCP with an associated Tale. Feel free to ask me for the draft if needed. I do even recommend it for reading, if you need to get a clearer picture of what I tried to sum up in 399 words here.

item.title: any suggestions for my SCP?: Re: any suggestions for my SCP?
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I'm not really a fan of the central narrative section; it feels…too expected and too focussed on the backstory of this. My general advice when writing a SCP is to forget about why it exists (and how the Foundation found it, a little). In general, backstory is not the most interesting angle because it happens a) before the foundation get involved (and so, before any of the PoV characters can be there) and b) it's just, not very interesting; and this suffers from this a lot since there's not really any way for the Foundation to know about the mans' gradual discovery of his powers, not a lot happens while he discovers them, and it's very temporally removed from the here and now and the people involved in the story.

Like, at the end of the day, you're trying to write an interesting short story about a weird thing, not an actual technical report on it; and so you really have to figure out why the weird thing existing is interesting and how it's existence affects the Foundation: like, do they use this man as like, a living transcriber? Do they run experiments on him? Does his ability pose difficulties because of some unforeseen aspect of them?

Part of my concern here is that the effects of the man are very…straightforward? One of the really hard parts of writing a scp is balancing the anomalous properties so that they're complex enough that you can do something interesting to explore what they mean whilst also not creating a big, overcomplex mess of properties that's hard for a reader to understand whilst also not being interesting. The Journey of Your First SCP: Part I talks about this a lot when it discusses 'depth vs complexity': at the moment, your anomaly is neither complex nor deep, and so there's not a lot of interesting things that it like…leads to a person being able to do; and I think this is why you're struggling a little to find the interesting thing here.

My suggestion would be to consider the emotions here: like, maybe there's an interesting angle where you can explore the effect that being in containment has on the man, and how it makes 'em feel; or perhaps you can figure out a reason for him to be in some like, really severe containment and so in turn, make a reader feel empathically sad at the Foundations treatment of him, or something.

It might be worth having a read of e.g. An exercise in narrative based SCPs and How Not to Walk Your Dog: An Essay on Pacing to really get a feel for like, how to do something interesting with the SCP idea.

item.title: SCP idea- Leviathan of The midnight Sun (Mitternachtsonne): Re: SCP idea- Leviathan of The midnight Sun (Mitternachtsonne)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

Gonna be honest: I don't really vibe with this. It feels…like a kinda stereotypical 'descent into madness' kinda story without really doing much to like, distinguish itself? Like it feels reminiscent of something like SCP-3000 or SCP-4391 but in a much more restrained way than the second and without the narrative heft of the first. In some ways, the uncertainty of the description of the SCP feels reminiscent of stuff like SCP-252 or a lot of antimemetic related stuff.

Beyond this, the way the narrative plays out feels…iunno, I think having it be framed as transcripts from the last surviving agent will really kill all the tension because we'll immediately know that everything the people do to try to survive will be futile and so it might be really hard to capture a readers interest. You might be able to manage a kinda, deep dread here where like, because we know it's futile, we just, are faced with the inevitability of the end; but it feels like that'd be really hard to do well.

On a very minor note, I have no idea how 'Midnight Sun' ties in here as a name.

Normally I'd offer some advice on how to improve this but I just, generally think it's not hugely something that appeals to me so you might find other reviewers are more receptive to it; or you might find that like, really leaning into the weirdness with it more, or like, doing more with it than just 'everyone ends up dying' would help?

item.title: Seeking Greenlight: SCP idea: Re: Seeking Greenlight: SCP idea
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I…really don't know about this? There's hints of intriguing elements: like the entity being invisible and harmless unless it's in atmosphere, and that the entity was one of the former crew, but the actual core of the narrative here just feels like an exceedingly generic murder monster story; and I feel like it could be fixed if this was just…shifted a little to be less horror orientated.

Like, consider if this was the story about someone being alone in space for so long that it changed them, and the focus was a lot more in how they react once they're no longer alone but they don't really know how to interact with the world any more; where perhaps you still keep the horror elements present but the motivation is this eldritch thing trying to interact with a world it's no longer part of and doing harm accidentally and that like, causing it to hate what it's become and stuff; and then you have this ending moment where like, everyone realises what has happened and it's like…bittersweet because they understand but they don't know what they can do to stop it?

Also…have you considered whether a SCP is the best format for this? It feels to me that a lot of the trappings of a SCP article (e.g., the ConProcs, leading with the Description) would make this story a lot more awkward to tell; whereas something like a tale from the perspective of one of the crew members might work a lot better. You wouldn't necessarily have to change a lot of the plot beats for this; including the presence of the Foundation, but it'd allow you to really focus on the important stuff and also to not worry about how to answer the question of 'how does anyone know what happened here'.

item.title: SCP-XXXX "The Frozen Wood": Re: SCP-XXXX "The Frozen Wood"
item.content:encoded:
1) While I love seeing thinking outside of the box, the spores would make it way too dangerous for too little advantage. On the other hand, it could be used for hiding secrets that The Foundation wants to hide. Of course, if they're using it, then it doesn't mean that other groups couldn't use it as well….

2) Conversely, even dead spores could be studied so that's not as big a problem as it may seem.

3) Your hook is just more description. There's a question of why this wood is important to the SCP-U as a whole; what niche does it fill, and what does it say about the universe as a whole? It's a neat idea, but why should people care about it beyond being a really scary place? It just needs an actual hook.

item.title: Rats that Spread Anamolies: Re: Rats that Spread Anamolies
item.content:encoded:
1) Kill the outlining. It works if you're separating points with paragraph breaks (like I'm doing) but actually makes your text harder to read and you just need commas; just write normal English minus the numbers.

2) If it's rats, then there will be a lot more than three victims. This means that The Foundation is going to have a far bigger problem than a couple of psychics. This is going to require a much more extreme solution. However, if the victims were linked to the rats somehow….

3) If the rats are acting as a swarm you may need to consider some form of extreme action. However, if the rats now have a hive intelligence of some sort (such as the legendary rat kings), then finding and eliminating those rat kings may help deal with the problem more efficiently.

4) You also need to consider that there are far more victims that like their powers, and have figured out how to use them subtlety. Also, they could consider working with The Foundation in order to learn more about anomalies and how to use them to their advantage. There are also obviously going to be those that will not want to be taken by The Foundation.

5) Overall, you don't have a bad idea. You just need to look at the possibility of large number of victims, and that some of them like their new powers.

item.title: SCP Idea: A Motel With An Elevator: Re: SCP Idea: A Motel With An Elevator

Overall, this is a fun idea.

1) Minor Quibble: It's not "non-existent" so much as a "pocket dimension". Just works better thematically.

2) Emphasize that curiosity is a major part of the hook. It's almost as if you are dancing around it, but you need to place it squarely in your sites.

3) You may want to pester some of the reviewers. This has some potential to be an SCP, but you need to bother them to get it reviewed.

item.title: Semi-Veil breaking Parawatch SCP idea: Re: Semi-Veil breaking Parawatch SCP idea
item.content:encoded:
+ Responses (Collapsed for size)
- Close

1) Agreed, will not add an interview log, but may add excerpts from the Parawatch forums to develop the story and Parawatches mindset.

2) Looking at the photo does nothing, but copying it does, creating a non-anomalous frog of the same type as the anomaly within the vicinity of the person who copied the photo. While this may not immediately be recognized anomalous it would some become apparent after a bit of experimenting. After the first Parawatch member discovered its' properties they sent the relevant instructions with the picture.

3)

Depending on your headcanon, the foundation has AI that sweep the internet for images all the time… why couldn't one of those merely delete the image as soon as its sent up?

Because, as you said, the photo isn't instantly recognizable as anomalous, and I doubt that the Foundation copies every Parawatch page for review. Additionally, it's my head cannon that Parawatch members take pictures of and post about weird animals all the time. After the Foundation picks up on the anomaly, taking it down won't do any good as many Parawatch members have recognized it as anomalous and stored it in their computers, continually re-posting it and spreading it through non-Parawatch channels.

Additionally I think it might make more sense to get some of the mods on the parawatch wiki to be double agents, and then they could call these things as off limits for members.

Maybe they do and maybe they tried. But the Parawatch members would just create new threads and posts to replace the ones banned or deleted by the mods, especially if they were certain the anomaly was real. And if by 'these things' you mean actual, demonstrable, online anomalous phenomena that the rest of Parawatch already know about I feel that the other Parawatchs would catch on very quickly that the mods were double-agents.

This could also introduce a meaty sub story about the Foundation trying to interfere directly with the Parawatch community which hasn't been done much before.

The entire concept of this article is the Foundation interfering with the Parawatch community in order to stop a breach of the veil. The Foundation frequently deletes posts and erases the memories of members, but never at this scale and never this directly. Some of the Parawatch forum excerpts will probably feature Foundation agents posing as members and trying to dismiss it as a hoax.

Also… I don't see the comedy, because you haven't really explained. It just sounds like someone sharing pics of a frog.

I find the concept of the Foundation almost being defeated and the veil shattered by Parawatch and a frog rather humorous. That being said, the article isn't primarily Comedy so I have changed 'Comedy' to 'Minor Comedy' in the Genre section.

item.title: Rats that Spread Anamolies: Rats that Spread Anamolies
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Drama

Elevator Pitch: 1) A cluster of genes on rats that effect their saliva and their longevity. 2) The effects to human exposure to the rat saliva grants psychic powers. 3) These psychic powers will appear on the effected at a later time due to a stressful situation. 4) both the rats themselves and the effected people must be contained as the latter's abilities cannot be removed and amnesiacs will only result in another potentially dangerous psychic outburst later.

Central Narrative: The article begins by describing the gene cluster on the rats and how it can be passed down, and the minor anomalous traits of the rats that do not relate to their effects on humans. It then goes into the impact it has on humans, how humans bitten develop psychic powers and the stressful circumstances that activated those traits. There is a chart of the victims of this SCP's containment and interviews of how they react to being forced in a cage. One of the victims is highly supportive of the SCP agent trying to solve the rat problem and is indoctrinated into the Foundation's worldview. The other is violent and refuses to accept captivity. The third is homeless and finds captivity in the Foundation, limiting but preferable to their previous life on the streets.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: How does the Foundation contain an anomaly when 1) it's both multiplying itself out of control 2) it blends in very well with non-anomalous common animals and 3) the effect it grants is potentially beneficial to ordinary citizens who would seek out out.

Additional Notes:

item.title: Anomalous-D: Re: Anomalous-D
item.content:encoded:
At this point I think your best bet is to reach out to authors of high-rated extradimensional SCP articles…and see what they think of what you have planned.

This is helpful, and exactly what I'll do.

I appreciate your taking the time to engage. I remain fascinated by the "possibilities" of this line of thinking and I'm willing to play with it until I can bring it to life.

Thanks again.

+ show block
– hide block

As a reader, I find the entire setup questionable, since not only is it odd that the Foundation thought that this "sadistic murderer" person was someone they could just lump in with all the other D-Class,

I have to admit, I find this confusing. I thought D-Class came off of death row. Who goes to death row but murderers? Lumping this disposable murder in with all the other disposable murderers is exactly what I thought the Foundation would do.

Taken directly from the wiki page on classes "…Class D personnel are expendable personnel used to handle extremely hazardous anomalies and are not allowed to come into contact with Class A or Class B personnel. Class D personnel are typically drawn worldwide from the ranks of prison inmates convicted of violent crimes, especially those on death row."

This describes him perfectly. And that he's repeatedly put in dangerous close contact with anomalies sounds like exactly what they're used for.

SCP-682 was written almost a decade ago and is one dangerous anomaly out of thousands. Most readers aren't going to take your premise seriously if you need to rely on super-old (and frankly, not great examples of current site standards) Series I articles to support your reasoning for the Foundation acting irrationally.

I am new to the concept of the SCP Foundation (learned about it two weeks ago). SCP-682 was one of my entry points into the storytelling. I do admit that I have no perspective on what people who have been immersed in it for years think of that particular anomaly, but as a new reader it honestly never occurred to me that it was in any way outdated.

item.title: New author need greenlight for idea: Re: New author need greenlight for idea
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block

Is a physical manifestation of anti-matter.

What does this mean? Anti-matter isn't an energy form… it is physical matter just, you know, anti-matter. Do you mean this is anti-matter that does not dissapate? Because a piece of anti-matter would negatively react to physical matter… for example they have created anti-matter at least a few times at CERN, but it "evaporated" fairly quickly I believe.

This entity is a sentient black fog.

See… this doesn't seem like a "physical manifestation"

It could be potentially useful to the foundation as it seems to interact with other SCPs in a positive way.

How? What ways? Also it positively reacts to ALL SCP anomalies? There's alot of different stuff on the wiki… many of which are just ideas.

Not much is known about anti-matter today which is why I think it would be cool to have an entity made of it to enhance the aspect of mystery.

While this is true, that not much is known… that just means you have to fill in the blanks. This is still fiction. So what does the anti-matter do to the people who have disappeared? What does the anti-matter do to anomalous objects? (I still think saying something has a universal effect on "SCPs" is problematic, because there's no one thing tying all SCPs together such that you could say this would happen every time, etc)

  • So this feels fairly thin, what is the article about? So there's this thing in a meteorite and people are disappearing… and? What happens in the article? Will the foundation merely catalogue this thing and then that's it? Because nowadays you need more narrative for an article to work…
